$comment: The words of the docs' Tools pages (docs/tools/…). Everything a person wrote about the tools is here, and workbench/playground/tool-docs.mjs only lays it out next to the reference it generates from the tools themselves. In the docs list every tool is a group under Tools (`name`), and its pages are the same kinds in the same order (`kinds`; AGENTS.md, 'How the Tools docs are organised'): OVERVIEW (what the tool is and does), SETUP (`setup`: what you need, the steps, how to see that it worked), then a generated REFERENCE page per kind the tool has (`pages`: commands, tools, shortcuts, settings, options, handler files). A fact has one home: write it on the page it belongs to and link there from `related`, don't repeat it. kinds: every kind of page, in the order of the docs list, with `nav` (its name in the list). index: the Tools page (lead; fit: the text under the 'one core' diagram; path: the caption of a handler's path; new: the line for newcomers). core, flow: the two diagrams. compare: the section of the Tools page that says what each tool can do, feature by feature (h, lead, note; its table is data/tools-compare.json, and it is the only place the tools are compared). tools: one entry per tool. name: the tool's group in the docs list. line: one line for the Tools page's table. summary: what the tool is, one or two sentences; explain a term a handler author may not know (language server, MCP) where it first comes up. facts: [name, text] pairs shown as a short list under the summary (what it runs on, what it needs, where its setup is). video (a demo in docs/videos) with videoLine; shots: gallery screenshots (docs/images/gallery) by name without -light/-dark, captions from the start page's gallery. pages: the tool's generated reference pages by kind; each has title, desc (for search engines and the docs list's filter), lead (one or two sentences on what the page lists) and optionally note (where the list comes from). What is on such a page comes from the tool itself, never from here; a commands page may add `what`, a line per command (by its id, or the menu entry's label) on what it does, where the name doesn't say it. sections: what the overview page says, each with a heading h and one or more of md (text), rows ([name, text] pairs as a table, with cols as its two headings) and pair (a two-box diagram: a and b are [title, line], caption is text). refNote: the small line under the generated reference, saying where it comes from. related: at most three links, shown last. setup: slug, title, desc, lead, needs (a list), steps (numbered), sections (before the check, e.g. one per system), verify (how to see that it worked), after (sections after the check), related. Text: `code`, a key in backticks (`F5`, `Ctrl+.`), **bold**, [links](https://…), (@site:<path>) for a page of the site, (@docs:<slug>#<part>) for a docs page, {repo} for this repository's address, {vscodeVersion} for the oldest VS Code the extension runs in (package.json engines); lines starting "- " are a list, "1. " numbered steps, and a ``` fence with a language is a code block. Reference text states what a thing is and does, in plain sentences; steps tell the reader what to do. Both read as if a person wrote them (AGENTS.md, Conventions).

index.lead: Tools for writing Nucleus Co-op handlers. Each one checks a handler for what Nucleus would reject or quietly ignore, shows what every player would get before a game is started, and has the docs for every option.
index.fit: They all run the same core, so a handler gets the same problems and the same Try it result in every tool. `ncdev` is that core as a program: the Notepad++ plugin, the language server and the MCP server are `ncdev` running in the background. The workbench and the VS Code extension carry the core themselves and don't need it.
index.path: Every tool covers writing, checking and Try it. Saving, testing in Nucleus Co-op and the debugger differ from tool to tool.
index.new: New to handlers? [Learn](@site:learn/) builds a first one with you, in the workbench.

commands.title: VS Code: commands
commands.desc: Every command the extension adds to VS Code, with its keys and what it does.
commands.lead: Every command the extension adds. They're in the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) under *Nucleus*. Two of them come with a key, and VS Code's Keyboard Shortcuts editor binds any of the others.

what.splitscreenme.whatsNew: Shows what changed in the version that's installed.
what.splitscreenme.newHandler: Asks for the game's name, its `.exe` and what the game needs, and writes a handler from a template.
what.splitscreenme.tryIt: Opens the Try it panel: what Nucleus Co-op would set up for each player, without starting the game.
what.splitscreenme.tryItSet: Changes how many players, which one has the keyboard and the monitor size Try it runs with. The panel's own links use it.
what.splitscreenme.tryItTestAll: Runs Try it for every player count, input setup and monitor size, and lists the combinations that fail.
what.splitscreenme.debugHandler: Starts VS Code's debugger on the handler: breakpoints, stepping and variables, player by player. It runs in the simulator, not in the game.
what.splitscreenme.explainLine: Says in plain words what the line under the cursor does.
what.splitscreenme.fixAll: Applies every fix that's safe to apply without asking.
what.splitscreenme.formatHandler: Tidies indentation, spacing, quotes and semicolons. It never moves anything to another line.
what.splitscreenme.packageHandler: Writes the handler and the files in its folder as one `.nc` package.
what.splitscreenme.installHandler: Copies the handler and its folder into Nucleus Co-op's `handlers` folder.
what.splitscreenme.testInNucleus: Installs the handler, then starts Nucleus Co-op with that game selected.
what.splitscreenme.openNucleusLog: Opens the log Nucleus Co-op writes while its debug log is switched on.
what.splitscreenme.browseHub: Searches the handlers on the Hub and opens one, to read or to start from.
what.splitscreenme.setupTypes: Adds a `jsconfig.json` and the type definitions to the folder, for tools that read those.
what.splitscreenme.setupAgents: Adds an `AGENTS.md`, the handler skill and `ncdev` to the folder, so an AI agent there can check and try its own work.
what.splitscreenme.lintWorkspace: Checks every handler in the open folder, not only the ones in tabs.
what.splitscreenme.openDocs: Lists the docs that are on the web, to open one in a browser.
what.splitscreenme.openInWorkbench: Opens the handler in the browser workbench.
what.splitscreenme.linkGameFolder: Picks the folder the game is installed in, so the handler's paths and file names are checked against it.
what.splitscreenme.showDocs: Opens the Docs panel, on the name under the cursor when there is one.
what.splitscreenme.docsSearch: Searches the docs for a name or a word.
what.splitscreenme.docsBack: Goes back a page in the Docs panel.
what.splitscreenme.docsVote: Records a 👍 or 👎 on a doc. The Docs panel's buttons use it.
what.splitscreenme.reportProblem: Opens the right report form on GitHub, with the version and settings filled in.
what.splitscreenme.requestFeature: Opens the feature request form on GitHub.
what.splitscreenme.reportCheck: Reports a check that flags code that's fine, with the rule and the line.
what.splitscreenme.reportTryIt: Reports a run where Nucleus Co-op did something else than Try it showed.

tools.line: Handler support in VS Code and VSCodium, with a Docs panel, Try it and a debugger.
tools.desc: What the VS Code extension is and what it adds to the editor.
tools.summary: The extension adds Nucleus Co-op handler support to VS Code and VSCodium. Problems are underlined while you type and come with fixes. It also has suggestions, docs, Try it, a debugger, and commands that package a handler, install it and start Nucleus Co-op with it.
facts: VS Code {vscodeVersion} or newer, and VSCodium
tools.videoLine: About a minute of problems, quick fixes, suggestions, parameter hints, the Docs panel and Try it.

sections.md: A `.js` file counts as a handler when it's in a `handlers` folder, or when its text looks like one. Handlers open in their own language mode, `nucleus-handler`, which keeps VS Code's JavaScript checks out of them. `splitscreenme.languageMode` changes that.

rows: Problems
Underlined in the code and listed in the Problems panel, while you type. `Ctrl+.` on one shows its fixes.
Suggestions and hover docs
Names, values and parameter hints as you type, and the docs of a name when you hover it. The hover links to the Docs panel.
Nucleus Docs panel
The API docs in a panel beside the code.
Try it
A panel with what each player gets: the window, the launch arguments and the file changes.
Debugger
`F5` steps through the handler in Run and Debug, with breakpoints and each player's variables.
New handler
**Nucleus: New Handler…** starts one from a template, with the game's name and .exe filled in.
Test in Nucleus Co-op

**Nucleus: Test in Nucleus Co-op** installs the handler and starts Nucleus with the game selected. Nucleus only reads handlers when it starts, so one that's already open is closed first, after asking.
AI agents
The extension registers the handler tools for Copilot and other agents in VS Code. They're the [MCP server](@docs:tools/mcp)'s tools.
AI-written docs
Some options have no official docs, so an AI wrote theirs from the Nucleus source. Those parts start with ✨ in hovers and sit in a tinted frame in the Docs panel.

tools.desc: What the Notepad++ plugin is and what it adds to the editor.

tools.videoLine: Under a minute. The checks, fixes, suggestions and docs, and the plugin's menu.

sections.md: The plugin starts `ncdev lsp` in the background and shows its answers the Notepad++ way. Problems are squiggles in the code and rows in a docked Problems panel. Hover docs and parameter hints are call tips. Suggestions come up in the auto-completion list.

rows: Problems
Underlined while you type. Hover one to read what's wrong, or press `Alt+Enter` to fix it.
New handler
**New handler…** in the menu starts one from a template.
Test in Nucleus Co-op
Installs the handler and starts Nucleus Co-op with the game selected. A Nucleus that's already open is closed first, after asking.
AI-written docs
Docs an AI wrote from the Nucleus source are marked [AI].

sections.md: The plugin is `NcDev.dll` in Notepad++'s `plugins\NcDev` folder. `NcDev.ini`, next to it, says where ncdev is. A copy of ncdev is kept in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ncdev`. Setup also adds one entry to Notepad++'s Run menu (in its `shortcuts.xml`). Where there's no plugin for your Notepad++ (ARM64), the names go into `autoCompletion\javascript.xml` instead, and the original is kept beside it as `javascript.xml.nucleus-backup`.

setup.title: Set up Notepad++
setup.desc: Install the plugin with ncdev.exe: a download and a double-click.
steps: Double-click it and choose **Set up Notepad++**. In a terminal the same thing is `ncdev setup notepad++`.
Allow it when Windows asks for permission. Notepad++'s folder isn't writable without it.
setup.verify: **Plugins › Nucleus Co-op handlers** is in the menu, and a mistake in the handler gets underlined.

after.md: It isn't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may stop it the first time. [What to do](@docs:tools/ncdev/setup#windows-smartscreen).

Give setup the folder. It needs no permission then.

```shell
.\ncdev setup notepad++ --path "C:\path\to\Notepad++"
```
`ncdev update` fetches the newest ncdev and refreshes the plugin with it.

tools.line: The tools as one command-line program.
tools.desc: What ncdev is: the tools as one command-line program.
tools.summary: `ncdev` is the handler tools as one command-line program. It checks and formats handlers, looks names up in the API, runs Try it and the debugger in a terminal, packages and installs handlers, starts Nucleus Co-op for a test, and searches the Hub.
facts: Windows (`ncdev.exe`), Linux x64 (`ncdev-linux-x64`), and anything with Node.js 18 or newer (`nucleus.js`)
`ncdev lsp` for editors, `ncdev dap` for debug clients, `ncdev mcp` for AI agents

sections.md:
```shell
ncdev lint handlers/                   # every problem in a folder of handlers
ncdev simulate MyGame.js --players 3   # Try it: each player's window, arguments and file changes
ncdev api Game.KillMutex               # an option's type, default and docs
ncdev lint --help                      # only that command's part of the help
```

`ncdev lint` exits with an error code when a handler has errors, which is what a script needs to stop on a broken one.

setup.title: Install ncdev
setup.desc: Download ncdev for Windows or Linux, or run it with Node.js.
setup.lead: `ncdev` is a single file, and nothing else gets installed with it. The workbench and the VS Code extension don't need it.

sections.md:
1. Download {download:ncdev.exe}.
2. Put it in a folder that's on your PATH. Or run it from its own folder, which in PowerShell is `.\ncdev`.

1. Download {download:ncdev-linux-x64}.
2. Make it runnable and put it on your PATH as `ncdev`:

```shell
chmod +x ncdev-linux-x64 && mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && mv ncdev-linux-x64 ~/.local/bin/ncdev
```

If `ncdev --version` isn't found after that, `~/.local/bin` isn't on your PATH yet. Add this line to your shell's startup file (`~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`) and open a new terminal:

```shell
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```
Download `nucleus.js` from [the newest release]({repo}/releases) and run it with Node.js 18 or newer. Write `node nucleus.js` wherever these pages say `ncdev`.

after.md: `ncdev.exe` isn't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may stop it the first time. Choose **More info › Run anyway**.
`ncdev update` replaces the standalone program with the newest release.
